name: THE SMOKESCREEN
mechanism: Coloured daytime smoke wall with winched camouflage hides
proposition: The sun is the lighting designer.
tagline: A wall of coloured smoke stands up in front of the stage, parts from the centre, and the two products are simply there, in clean sunlight.
audience: The stage is dressed as a calm, orderly forward position. Two large shapes sit under camouflage netting; nothing about them can be read. The chief guest walks to a field signal desk at the side of the stage and throws a single red lever. Along the stage front a line of floor units fires one after another, and a wall of dense coloured smoke climbs in front of the stage, one half saffron-amber, the other deep green, bright and saturated in the sun. For a few seconds the stage has gone. Then the wall opens from the centre like a pair of curtains being drawn, and the two products are standing on white plinths in full daylight, uncovered, with the LED wall awake behind them. The nets have vanished. Nobody saw them go.
hook: Every other reveal fights the daylight. This one needs it: coloured smoke is at its most vivid in direct sun, and the product is revealed in the best light there is.
stageDesign: The 56 x 20 ft deck is dressed sparingly in a field register: olive transit cases stacked at the upstage wings, a field signal desk with a whip aerial at stage right, no weapons, no sandbags, nothing theatrical about conflict. Each product stands on its white plinth under a camouflage hide: a garnished net over a shade-cloth liner, peaked on a light ridge prop above the product and pegged to weighted deck plates. Fourteen low floor smoke units sit in a straight line about 2 ft back from the stage lip, spanning 37 ft, joined to the signal desk by a visible field cable. Two wind machines sit low at centre stage behind the smoke line, aimed outward. Two more smoke units stand at the upstage corners for the closing marker plumes. The colours shown (saffron-amber and deep green) are placeholders for the event's two brand colours.
concealment: Two layers. Before the cue, each product is fully enclosed by its camouflage hide; the opaque liner under the net hides the shape from the front, both sides and above, so side seats and cameras see only a draped form. During the cue, the smoke wall hides the whole stage front for roughly 15 to 20 seconds in real time, which is when the hides are removed. The products are never seen half-covered.
guest: The chief guest throws one painted signal lever on the field desk at stage right, about 6 ft clear of the nearest smoke unit and on the upwind side. A lamp on the desk turns green. The lever is a ceremonial input: it gives the cue to the show-control operator and the licensed smoke technician, who fire the units. The guest then steps back toward the wing and watches the reveal from there, and walks in to stand between the products for the photograph once the stage is clear.

sequence.title: The position
sequence.detail: The stage sits quiet in daylight. Two camouflaged forms, a signal desk, a line of units along the stage front. The LED wall is black. A low, steady sound bed; a short spoken introduction.

sequence.title: The signal
sequence.detail: The chief guest is invited to the signal desk and throws the lever. The desk lamp turns green.

sequence.title: The screen goes up
sequence.detail: The floor units fire one after another across the stage, each with its own lamp, so the cue is seen to travel. The smoke wall builds from stage right to stage left: saffron-amber on one half, deep green on the other. Music lifts.

sequence.title: Inside the smoke
sequence.detail: With the stage hidden, two winch lines draw each hide back over its product and into a catch trough at the foot of the LED raiser. A spotter confirms both hides are clear. The LED wall wakes behind the smoke.

sequence.title: The parting
sequence.detail: The smoke units stop. Wind machines at centre push the wall outward to both sides; it opens from the middle like curtains. The two products appear in clean sunlight.

sequence.title: The hero frame
sequence.detail: Two slim marker plumes in the brand colours rise at the upstage corners, well behind and outside the products. The guest joins the products for the photograph. The last smoke drifts off the wings.

tech: Electrically fired coloured daytime smoke units (14 on the stage front, 2 upstage)
Licensed pyrotechnic / special-effects operator and firing system
Camouflage nets with opaque shade-cloth liners
Two electric winches with catch troughs
Wind meter and go / no-go procedure
Field signal desk with ceremonial lever
Show control and LED wall content
techDetail: The smoke is theatrical coloured daytime smoke from electrically fired cartridges in steel floor troughs, fired in sequence from a pyrotechnic firing system by a licensed operator; burn time is chosen at 30 to 45 seconds so the wall is self-ending. Water-based fog and CO2 cannot be coloured in daylight, so this effect is by nature a pyrotechnic product and is treated as one: product data sheets, a written risk assessment, exclusion distances, fire watch and permissions agreed in advance with the venue and local authorities. Each hide is a standard camouflage net sewn to a light shade-cloth liner, with a collapsible ridge prop so it never rests on the product; two lines on the upstage hem run to a small electric winch and the hide is dragged upstage, away from the audience, into a trough. The wind machines are standard drum fans on low cradles. The LED wall and audio run from show control on the same cue. The previz compresses the sequence to ten seconds; real running time is about ninety seconds.
feasibility: Wind decides this effect. In still air or a light breeze blowing from the audience toward the stage, the wall stands and clears cleanly. A breeze toward the audience is a no-go for the front line: coloured smoke carries dye that can mark light clothing and irritate eyes and throats, so it must not drift into the VIP rows. The front row needs to be set back from the smoke line by the distance the product data sheet and the operator require (plan for 10 m or more), which this layout must be checked against. The deck carpet and plinths near the units need protection from heat and dye. The nets must be proven to come off without snagging on the real product shapes, which are not yet known. Reset takes about 20 minutes (new cartridges, re-rig the hides), so a full rehearsal on site costs one set of cartridges.
mitigation: A wind meter is read at the stage before the cue and the operator has the final say. If the wind is toward the audience or above the agreed limit, the front smoke line is not fired: the hides are winched off in full view as a clean reveal in their own right, and only the two upstage corner plumes (downwind of everyone) give the colour. If the wind is across the stage, the wall is allowed to clear to one side instead of parting; it reads as one curtain being drawn. Low-residue, cool-burning cartridges are specified, units sit in steel troughs on fire-retardant matting, extinguishers and a fire watch stand at both wings, and the guest's desk is placed upwind. Each hide has a manual release and two stagehands ready to walk it off under cover of the smoke if a winch stalls. Asthma and smoke notices are given to guests in advance.
signature: Two walls of colour parting in full sun, and the products standing in the gap. It is the photograph of the day, and it can only be taken outdoors.
